replaceSection.heading: FOREWORD
items: The Ministry of Education in Zambia is pleased to share with you the exciting developments taking place in our education system through the implementation of the Competency-Based Curriculum. With the support of ZEPH, new and improved learner’s books and teacher’s guides have been developed to support learners and teachers. These books will help learners acquire the knowledge, skills and values needed to build our nation and become responsible citizens. This is a significant milestone for education in Zambia.

This Learner’s Book takes you further into the study of literature. It opens with the Concept of Literature and moves through Prose Fiction, Non-Fiction Prose, Drama and Poetry. It then traces African literature from the pre-colonial period, through the colonial, Negritude and post-colonial periods, to the contemporary period, before turning to Greek Epic Poetry, Greek Tragedy and Classical Greek Comedy.

These lessons will help you develop essential skills for life. You will learn to read closely, think critically, write and perform creatively and appreciate the cultures and experiences that literature records. Zambian and African texts sit alongside works from the wider world, so that you can relate what you read to your own life and community and become an active and engaged citizen.

I am proud of the Zambia Educational Publishing House (ZEPH) for the excellent work they do in producing quality educational materials. I encourage you to use this book diligently and to take part fully in its activities, so that you become a knowledgeable, responsible and proud Zambian who contributes to building a better Zambia.
Noriana Muneku (Ms.)
Permanent Secretary (Administration)
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION

deleteExact: choice and explain its moral lesson.
It suggests sacrifice, death and renewal, connecting the liberation struggle with the possibility of a new nation.
It reveals earlier events that influence characters' actions and relationships after independence.
The country is politically independent, yet corruption and inequality undermine the promise of freedom and social progress.
Dirt and decay suggest moral deterioration and the weakening of public responsibility.
Rain represents hope, renewal and the possibility of improved agricultural and economic conditions.
His experiences reveal the effects of racial discrimination and his search for freedom and human dignity.

Both novels question whether independence fulfils people’s expectations. Ngũgĩ explores the moral complexities of liberation, while Armah focuses on corruption and disillusionment in post-independence society.
Through agricultural initiatives and cooperation, the novel shows how shared knowledge and participation can help communities improve their livelihoods.

Symbolism is used in all three works to communicate wider ideas. The grain of wheat evokes sacrifice and renewal, dirt and decay suggest corruption, and rain clouds represent hope and the possibility of development.
